slides.title: Why Bring Liquid Cooling to an Air-Cooled Site?

cards.title: IT requirement
cards.body: Liquid cooling at the equipment.

cards.title: Facility starting point
cards.body: An existing air-cooled environment.

cards.title: Deployment condition
cards.body: Enough power, airflow, and heat-removal capacity.

slides.transcript:
Brazos addresses a practical deployment problem. The IT equipment needs liquid at its cooling interfaces, while the building already removes heat through air. Replacing the facility cooling distribution can be a substantial project. Brazos introduces a local liquid loop whose heat ultimately returns to that existing air system.

Google introduced Brazos in June twenty twenty-six. The OCP specification used here is version zero point seventy-five point four, effective September eleventh, twenty twenty-six. Its design requirements give us a more detailed basis for review than the original launch description.

The opportunity is incremental deployment, subject to site capacity. An available rack position does not establish sufficient electrical power, acceptable air temperature, or enough air-handling capacity. Those remain engineering questions. Start with a specific IT load and a specific location, then test whether the complete cooling path can support them.

slides.title: From IT Heat to the Hot Aisle

figure.alt: Moving warm-return and cooled-supply markers trace the closed IT liquid loop; separate inlet and exhaust air streams carry heat through Brazos to the facility air system.
figure.caption: Animated markers trace coolant circulation and air-side heat removal; motion speed is illustrative.

entries.text: IT adds heat to the closed liquid loop
Pumps maintain circulation to the IT load
Fans carry heat toward facility air handling

text_inventory.review_basis: Revised continuous-flow video: all five scene states and transition-adjacent decoded frames visually reviewed; actual HTTP playback changes within scenes, pauses to an identical frame, and follows real progress-bar clicks.

slides.transcript:
Begin at the equipment. Heat enters the coolant through the IT cooling interfaces. The liquid leaves the IT equipment warmer and returns toward the Brazos rack. This is a single-phase loop: the teaching model keeps the fluid liquid while its temperature changes.

Inside Brazos, the returning coolant passes through the radiator. The liquid and air remain separate streams. Heat transfers across the heat-exchanger surfaces. The radiator changes the coolant temperature; it does not send that coolant into a facility water loop.

The pumps circulate the cooled liquid back through the supply manifold and onward to the IT equipment. The closed path connects supply, IT load, return, and Brazos again. Its hydraulic resistance matters because circulation must provide the required flow through the actual installation.

On the air side, the rear fans draw inlet air through the chassis and discharge warmer air into the hot aisle. The room’s air-handling and heat-removal systems receive that heat. They remain part of the end-to-end cooling system, even though the IT uses liquid.

Keep both paths in your review. One carries coolant through the equipment and Brazos. The other carries air through the radiator and toward the facility cooling system. Brazos connects their thermal behavior. Reliable operation requires suitable conditions on both sides of that connection.

slides.title: Three Chassis Make the Brazos Sidecar

figure.alt: The reference sidecar combines three 11-OU chassis with supply and return manifolds. Source: Figure 3.0.
figure.caption: The reference sidecar combines three 11-OU chassis with supply and return manifolds. Source: Figure 3.0.

extract_from.method: Original embedded source image extracted without redrawing

entries.text: Total Thermal Capacity: 60 kW Nominal Load
Coolant compatibility: DI water or PG25
Operational simplicity of standard air systems

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review of the exact static asset

slides.transcript:
The reference sidecar contains three Brazos cooling chassis and integrated rack manifolds. Each chassis occupies eleven Open Units of rack height. Open Units describe this rack interface; they should not be substituted with conventional nineteen-inch rack-unit dimensions.

The supply manifold combines cooled liquid from the chassis and connects to the neighboring IT rack. The return manifold carries warm liquid back toward the cooling chassis. This makes the full rack assembly a useful boundary for flow and thermal-performance requirements.

The specification describes sixty kilowatts of nominal thermal load across the three units. Its overview illustration labels twenty kilowatts per chassis. Read those labels as the nominal reference arrangement, with the surrounding performance conditions still relevant. They are not proof that two remaining units can always support the original load after a third unit is removed.

This distinction prevents several common errors. A chassis dimension is not the full rack footprint. A fan-power value for one chassis is not total rack power. A rack curve with all installed pumps operating is not a failed-unit curve. When reviewing any claim, first identify whether it describes a component, one chassis, the Brazos rack, or the combined cooling installation.

slides.title: What Moves, Measures, and Protects the Coolant

figure.alt: Component placement supports circulation, heat transfer, sensing, and service access. Source: Figure 3.1.
figure.caption: Component placement supports circulation, heat transfer, sensing, and service access. Source: Figure 3.1.

extract_from.method: Original embedded source image extracted without redrawing

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review of the exact static asset

slides.transcript:
A Brazos chassis brings several functions together. The pumps move coolant around the external loop. Check valves limit reverse flow through a pump that is not operating. The radiator transfers heat to air, while the fan array establishes the air path through it.

The strainers capture particles before they can continue through sensitive parts of the circuit. The specification lists three-hundred-and-twenty-five mesh, or forty-four microns. This is a component requirement within the design, not a complete water-quality or cleaning strategy. The expansion tank accommodates the loop’s expansion behavior within its specified pressure and temperature limits.

Sensors make the system observable. Supply and return temperatures describe the liquid’s thermal change. Pressure measurements support differential-pressure control. Flow measurements help establish whether circulation matches the requirement. Inlet and outlet air temperatures connect the air-side condition to the heat-transfer task.

Leak detection adds another kind of evidence: whether liquid has escaped its intended path. It cannot replace pressure, flow, or temperature monitoring. A loop may have insufficient cooling without an external leak, and a leak signal does not by itself explain the remaining thermal capacity.

Review these functions as a connected system. Moving fluid, transferring heat, filtering, accommodating expansion, and detecting abnormal conditions each answer a different operating question.

slides.title: Locate the Facility Interface

cards.title: Brazos
cards.body: IT liquid → radiator → facility air.

cards.title: Facility-water CDU
cards.body: IT liquid → heat exchanger → facility water.

cards.title: Site review
cards.body: Verify the available path and capacity for the intended load.

slides.transcript:
Compare two ways of connecting liquid-cooled IT to the facility. In a liquid-to-liquid architecture, the coolant distribution unit transfers IT-loop heat into facility water. The facility-water conditions and connections become central integration requirements. The OCP Project Deschutes course explores that architecture in greater detail.

Brazos uses a liquid-to-air interface. The local IT loop transfers heat into air passing through the chassis. The design therefore removes the need for a facility-water connection at this cooling interface. It still needs a suitable air inlet, an exhaust path, and facility heat-removal capacity.

An air-cooled site may also have its own upstream water use or water-based equipment. The phrase liquid-to-air describes the Brazos interface; it does not establish a water-consumption claim for the entire facility. Similarly, avoiding one retrofit does not guarantee an available electrical or thermal margin.

For a candidate location, ask where the incoming air comes from and where the exhaust goes. Check whether the hot aisle can accept the flow and temperature, and whether nearby equipment remains within its limits. Then include the power used by cooling equipment in the site budget. The useful comparison is between complete heat-removal paths serving the same workload.

slides.title: Read the 60 kW Rack Rating in Context
rows: Maximum fan speed; zero hot-aisle back pressure
slides.transcript:
The overview table gives a useful starting point: sixty kilowatts of rack thermal load, nineteen gallons per minute of deionized-water flow, and twenty-five pounds per square inch of liquid pressure differential. It also lists an eight-degree approach temperature. These values describe the rack-level design target, not interchangeable ratings for every coolant or installation.

The airflow entry is approximately seventy-seven hundred cubic feet per minute at maximum fan speed, with zero hot-aisle back pressure. That condition matters. Additional resistance in the exhaust path can change the available flow. A site review therefore needs evidence for the installed air path rather than the headline airflow alone.

The detailed thermal table contains an unresolved condition issue. Its caption says nominal flow is twelve point eight gallons per minute. Yet the sixty-kilowatt column gives flow per kilowatt values that imply approximately nineteen point three to nineteen point five gallons per minute. Do not treat every load column as one constant-flow experiment.

The practical response is to keep the published values and their stated conditions visible, then request clarification before using that comparison to size an installation. A specification is useful evidence, and reading it carefully includes recognizing where two entries do not describe the same test condition.

slides.title: Airflow Has a Power Cost

figure.alt: Published chassis fan points show how airflow and fan power change with speed. Table 4.2; no interpolated performance model.
figure.caption: Published chassis fan points show how airflow and fan power change with speed. Table 4.2; no interpolated performance model.

entries.text: Each point is a stated test result, not a fitted curve.
Compare the cost of the additional airflow.
Verify the thermal need and air-path resistance

text_inventory.review_basis: All five final encoded scene states visually reviewed, with transition-adjacent frames and final held state. Distinct phrases transcribed from the matching deterministic sources.

slides.transcript:
Fan speed changes both airflow and electrical demand. The chassis data provides measured comparison points, which we will keep separate from the rack-level thermal table. Here, airflow is reported as standard cubic feet per minute, and power refers to the chassis fans.

At fifty-four percent fan speed, the table lists twelve hundred twenty-two standard cubic feet per minute and three hundred six watts of fan power. At sixty-five percent, the airflow rises to fifteen hundred fifty-five, while power rises to five hundred sixty-six watts. These are two operating points, not a promise about every installed condition.

At seventy-six percent speed, airflow is eighteen hundred seventy-seven and fan power is eight hundred eighty-four watts. At eighty-eight percent, those figures become twenty-two hundred thirteen and thirteen hundred twenty-seven watts. The gain in airflow comes with a growing electrical cost.

At full speed, the listed airflow reaches twenty-six hundred twenty-two standard cubic feet per minute, with nineteen hundred eighty-two watts of fan power. Compared with the fifty-four-percent point, that is a little over twice the airflow and roughly six and a half times the fan power. This comparison uses the table entries; it is not a fitted fan law.

Select a working point against the actual thermal requirement and air-path resistance. Maximum speed is available for particular conditions, including specified failure responses, but it carries a power and acoustic consequence. Keep chassis fan power distinct from pump power and total cooling-rack power when assembling the site budget.

slides.title: Available Pump Head Must Match the Load

figure.alt: Available pressure head and pump power are rack-level curves with three chassis and two parallel pumps per chassis. Figures 4.1–4.2.
figure.caption: Available pressure head and pump power are rack-level curves with three chassis and two parallel pumps per chassis. Figures 4.1–4.2.

extract_from.method: Original embedded plot images placed side-by-side without altering plot data

entries.text: Brazos aCDU Rack Level Dual Pump Hydraulic

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review of the exact static asset

slides.transcript:
A pump curve connects flow with the pressure head available to overcome the external hydraulic load. The Brazos rack curves are for three chassis, each containing two pumps operating in parallel. That population is part of the curve’s meaning.

Choose a pump-speed curve and follow it from low toward higher flow. Available differential pressure falls along the curve. The external loop also has a flow-dependent resistance from the IT equipment, hoses, manifolds, valves, and connections. The operating point must satisfy both the available pump head and that installed resistance.

Raising pump speed changes the available head, but it also changes electrical power. The separate pump-power plot supports that second question. Do not read an external pressure differential as an absolute system pressure, and do not substitute the expansion tank’s pressure rating for either quantity.

For deployment, obtain the required IT flow and its corresponding pressure drop, plus the remaining external loop losses. Use consistent units and the specified coolant conditions. Confirm that the installed system can operate at that point with the required control margin.

Finally, ask for the degraded-operation evidence. A curve with every installed pump running does not establish the performance after a pump or complete chassis becomes unavailable. That requires a corresponding test or qualified model under the failure condition being claimed.

slides.title: Approach Temperature Connects Air and Coolant

figure.alt: Illustrative arithmetic: 37 °C liquid supply − 29 °C inlet air = 8 °C approach. This is not a new measured test point.
figure.caption: Illustrative arithmetic: 37 °C liquid supply − 29 °C inlet air = 8 °C approach. This is not a new measured test point.

entries.text: Same approach + warmer inlet air → warmer liquid supply
Liquid return temperature rise is a separate quantity.

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review of the exact static asset

slides.transcript:
Approach temperature is the cold liquid supply temperature minus the cold inlet-air temperature. It describes how close the delivered coolant temperature comes to the entering air temperature at that operating point. It is not the temperature rise of the liquid across the IT equipment.

Consider a clearly illustrative case: inlet air at twenty-nine degrees Celsius and liquid supply at thirty-seven degrees. The approach is eight degrees. If the inlet air becomes warmer while that approach remains unchanged, the liquid supply becomes warmer by the same amount. Maintaining an approach target does not maintain one absolute coolant temperature.

The liquid return temperature introduces another constraint. It depends on the heat gained in the IT loop and on coolant flow and properties. The control system separately provides a maximum return-liquid temperature function. Keeping those quantities distinct helps explain why more than one limit may matter at once.

The specification includes nominal and modeling environmental conditions. Those ranges are not a blanket promise of full thermal capacity at every altitude and temperature. Likewise, compatibility with deionized water and a twenty-five-percent propylene glycol mixture does not prove identical performance with the two fluids.

For the site review, specify the actual entering air condition, coolant formulation, flow, and thermal load. Then obtain performance evidence at those conditions. Use the approach value as one part of the temperature budget, together with the IT equipment’s allowable supply and return conditions.

slides.title: Budget Cooling Power Alongside IT Power

cards.title: 60 kW
cards.body: Nominal connected rack thermal load.

cards.title: ≈4 kW per chassis
cards.body: Consumption limit; ≈12 kW for three chassis.

cards.title: 5 kW per chassis
cards.body: Electrical design capability, a different requirement.

slides.transcript:
Cooling equipment consumes electricity while it removes heat from the IT load. The Brazos electrical requirements distinguish two values for one chassis. The electrical design must support five thousand watts maximum, while total consumption is limited to approximately four thousand watts per chassis. A three-chassis cooling rack is therefore approximately twelve kilowatts at that stated consumption limit.

Those are electrical quantities. The sixty-kilowatt nominal rating describes thermal load from the connected IT equipment. It is not the cooling rack’s electrical input, and the five-kilowatt design requirement should not replace the stated consumption limit in a routine operating claim.

For an initial illustrative budget, sixty kilowatts transferred from the IT liquid loop plus twelve kilowatts of cooling electrical input gives approximately seventy-two kilowatts. This is a high-budget case using the stated limit, not a measured typical operating point. Other IT heat and site loads must be added where applicable.

The detailed busbar requirements list a nominal fifty-four point five volts, a minimum of forty volts, and a maximum of fifty-nine point five volts, with specified transient conditions. The overview rounds the input range to forty through sixty volts. Use the detailed requirements when reviewing the electrical interface.

A sound budget identifies the load, the cooling operating point, electrical headroom, and the destination of the heat. It does not count the thermal rating as free capacity independent of the equipment required to deliver it.

slides.title: Check the Full Installation Envelope

figure.alt: Main chassis volume, specified protrusions, and working space are separate checks. Dimensions are not a scale installation drawing.
figure.caption: Main chassis volume, specified protrusions, and working space are separate checks. Dimensions are not a scale installation drawing.

entries.text: Service envelope: activities within 48 in in front
Also assess the specified rear fan access.

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review of the exact static asset

slides.transcript:
The eleven-Open-Unit chassis height is only the start of a fit review. The specification defines a keep-in volume, exclusions, front and rear protrusions, and use-specific exceptions. The main nominal dimensions are five hundred sixty-five point five millimeters wide, five hundred twenty-five high, and six hundred nine point six deep.

The depth of that main volume is not the complete installed depth. Later requirements include connector and handle exceptions, with an actual total depth stated as eight hundred thirteen point seven millimeters. Check the full geometry for the selected configuration, including hose routing and access to the front components.

The design covers the Z2 rack and the proprietary SH interface. It uses an ORV2-compatible power connector with specified enhanced features, even though the overall deployment uses the ORV3 form factor. The rack label alone does not prove connector position or adapter compatibility.

Service adds another envelope. The specified maintenance and replacement activities, including lift-assist use, must fit within forty-eight inches in front of the rack. Fans also have rear service provisions, so assess the complete access arrangement. The dry and filled weights require appropriate handling equipment and the supplier’s approved method.

For acceptance, review the applicable drawing revision, adapters, busbar mating, manifold clearances, and service access together. A dimensional match to the main chassis box is not enough to establish a serviceable installation.

slides.title: Connect the Manifolds and Compatible Coolant

figure.alt: Supply and return manifolds connect the three chassis to the neighboring IT rack. Source: Figure 8.2-1.
figure.caption: Supply and return manifolds connect the three chassis to the neighboring IT rack. Source: Figure 8.2-1.

extract_from.method: Original embedded source image extracted without redrawing

entries.text: Hose w/ FD83 to machine rack(s)

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review after compositing the original transparent artwork onto the white PDF background

slides.transcript:
Viewed from the front, the rack’s supply manifold is on the right and the return manifold is on the left. Each connects to the three cooling chassis and combines the flow into a connection near the top for the neighboring IT rack. Passive air vents and their quick-disconnect interfaces are part of the arrangement.

Connection geometry matters beyond the connector name. Check hose routing, front protrusions, swivel and elbow requirements, and the access needed for serviceable parts. Where the specification identifies a named quick-disconnect as an example, do not turn that example into an unsupported sole-source requirement. The specified interface and qualification requirements still apply.

Wetted materials must be compatible with deionized water and PG25, the twenty-five-percent propylene glycol mixture. The document lists examples of treated-water and glycol formulations and explicitly excludes nickel-plated brass from the system. A fluid-family label alone does not establish compatibility with every seal, metal, hose, or component in the installed loop.

Use the linked Cooling Fluids in Direct Liquid Cooling course for a deeper treatment of chemistry, material compatibility, sampling, and fluid health. For Brazos, obtain the exact approved formulation and the supplier’s installation and commissioning instructions. Do not infer a mixing or dosing procedure from a material-compatibility statement.

The acceptance question is whether the actual fluid, actual wetted materials, and actual liquid interfaces form a qualified system.

slides.title: Hot-Swappable Parts Do Not Guarantee Rack Redundancy

cards.title: Component service
cards.body: Use the qualified replacement procedure for that FRU.

cards.title: Whole-chassis service
cards.body: Remaining connected units must support the actual IT load.

cards.title: Replacement compatibility
cards.body: Same-vendor chassis rack; qualified and correctly keyed FRUs.

slides.transcript:
Field-replaceable components support maintainability, but different service actions have different consequences. The design includes hot-swappable pumps and fans, along with other serviceable assemblies. The supplier’s approved procedure determines the handling, isolation, and checks for the particular action.

Removing a complete chassis is a larger change. Section twelve point one states that the whole unit may be hot-swapped only when the cooled IT load is below the capability of the other connected Brazos units on the shared manifold. Otherwise, the affected IT equipment may need to be powered down because cooling would be unavailable.

That condition requires more than dividing a nominal rack rating by three. Verify the remaining units’ thermal and hydraulic capability under the actual air, coolant, and load conditions. Include the control response during removal and return to service. A three-unit arrangement alone does not establish a sixty-kilowatt N+1 claim.

Parts qualification is another boundary. The specification allows component second sourcing within a qualified assembly, while requiring all three chassis in one Brazos rack to come from the same vendor. It also calls for physical keying to prevent incorrect cross-vendor field-replaceable-unit insertion.

Treat service continuity as a claim that needs evidence. Name the component or chassis being removed, identify the remaining cooling path and capacity, and verify the procedure for that exact implementation.

slides.title: Service One Chassis While Protecting the Rack

figure.alt: The interlock limits chassis extension; independent leak detection and remaining cooling capacity are separate requirements.
figure.caption: The interlock limits chassis extension; independent leak detection and remaining cooling capacity are separate requirements.

entries.text: Conceptual service arrangement · follow the qualified procedure
Stability + leak coverage + remaining cooling capacity

text_inventory.review_basis: All five final encoded scene states visually reviewed, with transition-adjacent frames and final held state. Distinct phrases transcribed from the matching deterministic sources.

slides.transcript:
Consider the physical service arrangement with three chassis mounted on slides. Each unit is heavy, and extending a chassis moves its load forward. The rack must remain stable throughout the approved service activity. The diagram explains the interlock principle; it is not a replacement sequence.

When one chassis extends, the interlock must prevent another chassis from extending at the same time. This mechanism is separate from the securing features used to hold equipment in place. Simply releasing a mounting restraint must not allow an operator to defeat the one-chassis condition accidentally.

A second extension attempt remains blocked while the first unit is out. This protects against the tipping condition the interlock is designed to prevent. The specification also requires warnings and validation of the mechanism. A functioning drawing is not evidence that a particular rack has passed those tests.

Leak coverage is an independent requirement. Each chassis needs its own detection, including an internal cable and an external connection for the specified coverage. Minor internal leaks must be contained and routed toward controlled front drainage. The specification does not permit one chassis’s leak detection to be daisy-chained through another.

Bring these checks together without confusing their purposes. The interlock addresses physical extension and rack stability. Detection and drainage address escaped liquid. Cooling continuity still depends on the remaining equipment and the approved service plan. Satisfying one of these conditions does not prove the others.

slides.title: Decide What a Service Plan Still Needs

cards.title: Capacity evidence
cards.body: Actual load, remaining units, and transient response.

cards.title: Qualified method
cards.body: Supplier procedure, access, interlock, and handling.

cards.title: Return-to-service evidence
cards.body: Correct parts, traceability, and operating checks.

slides.transcript:
A proposed service plan says: remove one chassis, replace a failed assembly, and return the unit to the rack while the IT load continues. Before accepting that plan, separate what has been stated from what has been demonstrated.

First, establish the load and the remaining cooling capability. The plan needs evidence at the relevant air and liquid conditions, including flow and control response. A nominal full-rack capacity statement does not answer the reduced-equipment question.

Second, verify the physical method. The rack, slides, interlock, lift assist, and working space must support the intended activity. The supplier’s procedure must specify how the actual unit is handled and how it is made ready for removal and return. Do not invent those steps from the component drawing.

Third, confirm the replacement assembly and its traceability. A similar-looking part is not evidence of approved compatibility. Check the qualified part identity, connector and keying arrangement, and the documentation for the installed vendor’s implementation.

Finally, identify how success will be observed. The plan should name the applicable status, leak, pressure, temperature, and flow checks, together with the expected service outcome. If the evidence is incomplete, record an open action with an owner. That is a useful engineering decision, not a failure to understand the specification.

slides.title: Two Default Loops and Protective Limits

figure.alt: Pumps normally regulate liquid differential pressure; fans regulate approach. Configurable hot-side temperature limits override other automatic modes.
figure.caption: Pumps normally regulate liquid differential pressure; fans regulate approach. Configurable hot-side temperature limits override other automatic modes.

entries.text: Return liquid: 55 °C default     ·     Exhaust air: 50 °C default

text_inventory.review_basis: Full-resolution visual review of the exact static asset

slides.transcript:
The default pump loop regulates a pressure differential between liquid supply and return. The controller adjusts pump speed to maintain that setpoint. This supports the hydraulic task, while other selectable pump modes provide different control choices for a qualified application.

The default fan loop regulates approach temperature: cold liquid supply minus cold inlet air. The controller changes fan speed to maintain that difference. Because inlet air can vary, a fixed approach does not guarantee a fixed absolute coolant temperature.

Two additional functions limit hot-side temperatures. The specified default maximum for returning liquid is fifty-five degrees Celsius. The default maximum for exhaust air is fifty degrees Celsius. Both are configurable and enabled by default. When their specified threshold is reached, these functions take precedence over the other automatic control modes.

Redundant sensors support the controls, but disagreement also needs defined handling. The specification directs the pump calculation toward the lower reported pressure differential when the paired readings exceed their expected agreement. For fans, the corresponding rule uses the greater reported approach temperature. These choices should be demonstrated in validation, not assumed from the presence of duplicate sensors.

The practical distinction is between the quantity being regulated, an overriding temperature constraint, and a fault response. They answer different questions. A control review should identify the sensor inputs, the active mode, its setpoint, and the expected behavior when readings or equipment become abnormal.

slides.title: From Startup to Supervisory Handover

figure.alt: Startup, reboot, supervisory timeout, and fault response are distinct control cases. Timing is explanatory; site-specific behavior requires validation.
figure.caption: Startup, reboot, supervisory timeout, and fault response are distinct control cases. Timing is explanatory; site-specific behavior requires validation.

entries.text: Liquid presence is an enable condition.
Two different cases; do not collapse them into one reset rule.
Controller decrements timeout once per second
Maintain speeds within the specified bounds
Manual-mode behavior and control priorities need explicit validation.

text_inventory.review_basis: All five final encoded scene states visually reviewed, with transition-adjacent frames and final held state. Distinct phrases transcribed from the matching deterministic sources.

slides.transcript:
Start with the liquid-presence condition. Pumps must not turn on simply because the power board is inserted into the live rack busbar. The controller must verify liquid using the specified suction-pressure or liquid-level evidence before enabling the pump drives. This prevents dry running.

Initial startup and reboot are different cases. The configurable initial defaults are manual mode with pump and fan speeds at twenty-five percent. A reboot after a power interruption or software update must retain the controller’s preceding state. Do not treat the initial default as a command to reset every restart to manual operation.

During normal automatic operation, the local controller regulates the selected pump and fan variables. A tier-two supervisory system may impose minimum and maximum speed bounds. To enter that mode, it writes a positive timeout value. The local controller decrements that value once each second.

While the timeout remains positive, the controller applies the supervisory bounds and slews toward them at a safe rate where necessary. When the timeout reaches zero, it exits tier-two operation with a smooth transfer back to local control. The timeout is a control-handover mechanism, not proof of a deployed facility optimization service.

Failures are separate branches. The specification defines default full-speed responses for particular sensor, communication, pump, or fan failures, and also describes a manual mode that overrides failsafe conditions. Validate those state-specific behaviors, including their interaction with the installed controls. Avoid assuming every abnormal condition has the same response or inventing an undocumented priority rule.

slides.title: Separate Local, Telemetry, and Management Interfaces

cards.title: Local interface
cards.body: HMI: status, configuration, and local interaction.

cards.title: Remote interfaces
cards.body: Modbus TCP telemetry; Redfish configuration and metrics.

cards.title: Firmware lifecycle
cards.body: Dual images, update checks, and implementation-specific integration.

slides.transcript:
The control system exposes different interfaces for different purposes. The front-panel human-machine interface, or HMI, supports local interaction. The network-facing controller supports remote visibility and control, with requirements for concurrent Internet Protocol versions four and six.

The specification identifies Modbus over TCP for mapped telemetry and register access. It also requires a Redfish management interface for configuration, asset information, and real-time sensor metrics. Do not collapse those into one protocol or assume their data models and permissions are identical.

The network requirements include a front Ethernet connection and a specified vendor-class identifier in DHCP requests. A service USB port must be disable-capable. These details belong in the integration and configuration evidence for the actual controller.

Firmware updating is another function. The specification calls for two image partitions and checks before accepting an update. Its detailed update interface uses a separate HTTP service and explicitly describes unauthenticated requests. A checksum detects specified corruption; it does not establish access control or image authenticity.

For this course, focus on the review questions: which interface owns the function, what data is available, how is it configured, and what has been validated for the deployment? Verify implementation-specific endpoints and network controls against the approved integration plan before any operational use.

slides.title: What Must Be Demonstrated Before Acceptance?

cards.title: Performance and response
cards.body: Representative conditions, load changes, and failure cases.

cards.title: Physical and compliance evidence
cards.body: Fit, service trials, safety, and EMC documentation.

cards.title: Quality and traceability
cards.body: Qualified parts, reliability tests, records, and open-action ownership.

slides.transcript:
A requirements list becomes useful deployment evidence when the supplier demonstrates the behavior of the delivered system. Start with thermal and hydraulic performance under the intended conditions. Include inlet air, exhaust resistance, coolant, flow, load, and the equipment population used in the test.

Next, review dynamic and abnormal cases. The validation section includes heat-load changes, fan and pump failures, control failures, telemetry loss, and leak detection. The purpose is to connect a stimulus to an observed response and verify the monitoring that reports it. A nominal steady-state result does not cover all of those cases.

Physical service trials provide a different kind of evidence. Fit, removal, replacement, handling, connector cycling, and return to service need demonstration in the relevant arrangement. Safety, electromagnetic compatibility, and regulatory documentation must apply to the delivered implementation and its operating environment.

Reliability and manufacturing records complete the picture. The specification calls for component and system testing, traceability, and qualification across development stages. Exact test conditions and acceptance criteria belong in the approved test plan, especially where the specification’s tables contain inconsistent or incomplete entries.

For each open item, record the claim, the applicable requirement, the evidence, and an owner for the remaining action. Acceptance is a documented judgment about a particular implementation and site. It is not established by the specification’s existence or by a supplier’s headline capacity statement.

slides.title: Is This Air-Cooled Site Ready for Brazos?

cards.title: Known
cards.body: 60 kW connected liquid load; sidecar space identified.

cards.title: Unresolved
cards.body: Air and power margins, hydraulic conditions, and degraded capacity.

cards.title: Decision
cards.body: Hold acceptance; assign owners and collect the missing evidence.

slides.transcript:
Apply the course to a fictional proposal. The connected IT liquid load is sixty kilowatts. The site has identified floor space for a Brazos sidecar and points to the nominal rack rating. The proposal also assumes that IT service will continue while one chassis is replaced.

Some facts are useful, but the decision is not yet complete. The nominal rating and space allocation establish a starting point. They do not show the actual inlet-air condition, the exhaust resistance, or the room’s remaining heat-removal capacity. Nor do they include the cooling electrical demand and any other relevant loads.

The liquid side also needs evidence. Confirm the required flow and pressure drop, the selected coolant formulation, and the compatibility of the installed wetted materials and connectors. Verify the complete installation envelope, hose routing, and service access against the applicable drawings and procedures.

The service assumption is especially important. Ask for demonstrated capability with the relevant chassis unavailable at the intended load and operating conditions. Identify the remaining flow paths and the controller’s response. Without that evidence, the whole-chassis service-continuity claim remains unresolved.

Finally, check that monitoring and acceptance records cover the installed system. Who owns each alarm or control interface? Which failure tests were completed? Which supplier procedures and qualified parts will the operations team use?

The justified decision is to hold deployment acceptance until these gaps are closed, with named owners and evidence requirements. This does not say Brazos is unsuitable. It says the available information is insufficient to support this particular proposal. That distinction is the central skill: turn an attractive architecture into a qualified, evidence-based decision.

term_glossary.tooltip: Coolant distribution unit: equipment that circulates coolant and transfers heat across the cooling-system interface. Brazos uses a liquid-to-air interface.
Open Unit: the rack-height increment used by Open Rack. Brazos occupies 11 OU per chassis; this is not the conventional 19-inch rack unit.
Field-replaceable unit: an assembly intended to be replaced in the field using the qualified service procedure. Replacement compatibility must be established.
The 25% propylene glycol coolant mixture identified in the Brazos compatibility requirements. The actual formulation and wetted materials still require qualification.
The pressure difference between liquid supply and return. In Brazos this is the default regulated pump quantity; it is distinct from absolute system pressure.
Cold liquid supply temperature minus cold inlet-air temperature. It is the default fan-control quantity, not the liquid temperature rise across the IT load.
Standard cubic feet per minute: airflow expressed at a standard reference condition. Brazos Table 4.2 reports chassis airflow in this unit.
Human-machine interface: the local front-panel interface for status, configuration, and interaction with the controller.
Tier-two supervisory control: a supervisory system supplies speed bounds while its positive timeout remains active. Expiry returns control smoothly to the local controller.
Electromagnetic compatibility: operation within the applicable electromagnetic emission and immunity requirements.

lms_catalog.short_description: Evaluate Brazos liquid-to-air cooling, performance limits, rack integration, controls, and deployment readiness.
lms_catalog.overview: Learn how OCP Project Brazos supports liquid-cooled IT in an air-cooled facility, and how to assess whether a particular installation is ready. Follow the heat path, interpret performance conditions, examine integration and service requirements, and use control and validation evidence to make a qualified deployment decision. The course is based on specification v0.75.4, effective September 11, 2026, with Google's June 2026 announcement providing context.

modules.summary: Trace the closed liquid loop and the facility air path. Distinguish chassis components, the three-chassis sidecar, and the site's continuing heat-removal responsibility.
Interpret nominal thermal capacity, airflow, pump curves, approach temperature, and cooling electrical power with their published boundaries and conditions.
Review installation geometry, liquid connections, compatible fluids, qualified parts, rack interlocks, leak detection, and conditional whole-chassis service continuity.
Explain default control loops, startup and supervisory handover, interface roles, fault behavior, and the evidence required to accept a deployment.
